article.body_html:
Ride-hailing versus a rental bike for a week in Hanoi is a question you can answer with arithmetic instead of a gut feeling. The answer depends on how many separate rides you will really take, what each one costs on the app, and what a bike would cost once you add fuel, parking and the days it might sit unused.

Step 1: turn your plans into a count of legs

List every outing you expect each day and count each leg separately, including the way back. Dinner out, a morning at a museum and an evening walk are three outings, but up to six legs once you count every ride home. Use a worksheet like this for the whole week:

DayOutings plannedLegs (including returns)Fare from the app
Day 1Arrive, dinner nearby2[your figure]
Day 2Museum, lunch, evening walk6[your figure]
Day 3Half-day outside the centre3[your figure]
Other days.........

Add up the last two columns to get your legs and your ride-hailing cost for the week. If you are not sure, plan a realistic number of legs rather than an optimistic one.

Step 2: price a ride from the app, not from memory

Fares vary by distance, time of day and weather, and they often rise at rush hour or in the rain. The reliable way is to open the app and look up a few of your real routes at the times you will travel, then enter each leg's fare in the last column. If your legs are all about the same length you can use one typical fare for every leg, as the example below does. Do not use someone else's average; use your own routes.

Step 3: price the bike honestly

Reference prices at Thuê xe máy Nguyễn Hà for a manual bike by the week run from 700,000 to 800,000 VND, for an automatic bike from 600,000 to 1,000,000 VND, and for an electric bike from 600,000 to 800,000 VND; these are reference prices only, so confirm the bike and the rate before booking. Rent is only part of the cost, so add the items below, which you estimate yourself:

  • fuel for the distance you expect to ride (or charging, for an electric bike);
  • parking at hotels, cafes and attractions that charge for it;
  • the days you may not ride, such as a day of heavy rain or a tired morning, because you still pay for them;
  • if you want the bike for longer than booked, ask the shop to extend it: Thuê xe máy Nguyễn Hà charges an extension fee of 20,000 VND per hour, and more than 6 hours is charged as one rental day, so confirm how it applies to your booking.

A worked example with made-up numbers

This is only an illustration with invented figures, so replace them with yours. Suppose your plan has 23 legs in the week. Suppose an average ride costs 50,000 VND on the app: 23 rides come to 1,150,000 VND. Suppose a manual bike at the reference weekly rate plus an estimate of 150,000 VND for fuel and parking comes to between 850,000 and 950,000 VND. In this example, the bike is cheaper by roughly 200,000 to 300,000 VND. The table shows how the answer changes with the fare. It lists the number of legs at which ride-hailing starts to cost as much as the bike.

Average ride (illustration)Bike total 850,000 VNDBike total 950,000 VND
35,000 VND25 legs28 legs
50,000 VND17 legs19 legs
70,000 VND13 legs14 legs

Read it like this: if your plan has fewer legs than the number in the table, ride-hailing is cheaper on cost alone; at that many legs or more, the bike costs the same or less. A plan with 23 legs is above the break-even at the middle and top fares and below it at the lowest.

Adjust for the days the bike sits idle

A rental that sits unused still costs the same, and the legs you would have ridden on an idle day still have to be paid for another way. If you expect idle days, such as a day of heavy rain, a tired morning or an evening with drinks, price those legs on the app and add them to the bike total before you compare.

In the illustration, suppose two idle days hold about six of the 23 legs. At 50,000 VND each that is 300,000 VND, so the bike total becomes 1,150,000 to 1,250,000 VND against 1,150,000 VND for all 23 legs by app. The saving from the first comparison disappears, which is why this step is worth doing.

What a worksheet cannot tell you

  • Confidence: if you have not ridden for a long time, a bike is not the cheaper option if you would not feel safe on it. The guide to motorbike riding tips for first-time riders covers what to practise first.
  • Parking and bags: a hotel with no parking, or a plan that needs you to leave the bike unattended, changes the sum.
  • Waiting: ride-hailing at peak times or in the rain can mean long waits, which cost time you cannot get back.
  • Evenings: if you plan to drink, ride-hailing is the sensible choice for that evening whatever the sum says.
  • Flexibility: a bike lets you stop where you like; an app turns every stop into a new ride.

A simple way to decide

Fill in the worksheet, price both options, add the legs that fall on idle days, compare the totals and then ask whether any of the points above should override the result. A mixed plan can work: a bike for the days with many short stops, and ride-hailing for the evenings or the rainy days. For a day-by-day view of fuel, parking and food, the Hanoi motorbike day budget worksheet covers it, and the motorbike rental prices in Hanoi page lists the shop's reference prices.
